entries.title: France's Macron, Spain's Sanchez welcome idea of UK rejoining EU after Burnham remarks
entries.summary: During a visit to Spain, France's Emmanuel Macron said it would be "good news" if the UK moves towards the EU, with Pedro Sanchez also embracing the idea. UK PM Andy Burnham has not ruled out rejoining the bloc.
entries.content:
Europe

France, Spain welcome idea of UK rejoining EU

September 30, 2026

During a visit to Spain, France's Emmanuel Macron said it would be "good news" if the UK moves towards the EU, with Pedro Sanchez also embracing the idea. UK PM Andy Burnham has not ruled out rejoining the bloc.

French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Wednesday welcomed the idea of the United Kingdom rejoining the European Union. 

During a visit to Madrid while meeting with Sanchez, Macron reacted to the idea of a UK rejoin with two words in English: "Welcome back."

"If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news both for his country and for Europeans," Macron continued in French.

At the same time, Macron said the UK cannot take an a la carte approach to its relationship with the EU, while remaining outside the bloc.

"You cannot choose between the freedoms of the union and decide to take what suits us and not the rest," he said.

Sanchez said the UK's decision to leave the EU as a result of a referendum in 2016 is "a huge loss, both for the British population and for the whole European project."

The Spanish prime minister said if the UK indeed does try to rejoin the EU, "then of course Spain would applaud it and open its arms again to a brotherly people."

In a separate statement from the EU, European Commission spokesperson Balazs Ujvari said: "The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward."

"We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward," Ujvari said.

Burnham: UK should consider options in regards to EU ties

In an interview with the BBC earlier on Wednesday, UK Prime Minister  Andy Burnham said Britain should look at various options when it comes to the relationship with the EU.

"We could stay as we are. That's definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay," Burnham said, while saying one option would be to "go all the way."

Other possibilities might include rejoining the EU's single market or a customs union between the two sides, he said.

During a speech at the annual Labour Party conference on Tuesday, Burnham said that "Brexit has done more harm than good." He added he would set out "different options" for the UK-EU relationship closer to a summit between the two sides in November.

Such a decision to move closer or rejoin the EU could open up a tense political debate in the UK.

Although recent public surveys suggest that the majority of Britons back rejoining, the idea of adopting the Euro currency or contributing to the EU budget would likely spark fierce backlash. Moreover, the UK is unlikely to receive the same exemptions it had when it was previously a member of the EU.

For now, Burnham is committed to the 2024 Labour Party manifesto, which ruled out rejoining the EU and other elements such as returning to the EU single market. However, Burnham could push Labour for a closer approach to the EU in the next general election, which is slated for no later than August 2029.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Are the Houthis winning against Saudi Arabia?
entries.summary: It's unclear how the Saudis can defuse the threat presented by the Houthis in next-door Yemen or who they can turn to for help. The US isn't interested, the Europeans are hedging and nobody wants open conflict with Iran.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Are the Houthis winning against Saudi Arabia?

September 30, 2026

It's unclear how the Saudis can defuse the threat presented by the Houthis in next-door Yemen or who they can turn to for help. The US isn't interested, the Europeans are hedging and nobody wants open conflict with Iran.

Last week, some students in Saudi Arabia were told they should stay at home and attend classes online, due to continued threats from attacks by the Houthi group in neighboring Yemen. But the very next day, they were given the all-clear and allowed to return to school in person.

The conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen seems to have become part of everyday life in Saudi Arabia. After a period of comparative calm, the Houthis have been ramping up attacks on the country, starting July, and have fired many missiles and drones over the border.

Over recent weeks, the Houthi militia have also pushed further into Yemen, taking more control of the Yemeni coast and several islands in the Red Sea. This means they can oversee maritime traffic in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

The renewed Houthi attacks endanger Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's ambitious project to move the kingdom away from its dependence on oil revenues, which was conceived by Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. To make Vision 2030 a reality, Saudi Arabia needs stability — but right now, the outlook is moving in the opposite direction.

"The escalation in Yemen is drawing the Saudis deeper into the regional war, a war that Saudi Arabia actually wanted to prevent," said Marcus Schneider, who heads the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Regional Peace and Security Project in the Middle East.

Impact on world's energy

Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure is particularly vulnerable to Houthi attacks, which have already disrupted the so-called East-West pipeline, which runs for over 1,200 kilometers. It was being used to transport oil after other routes, such as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, became precarious due to fighting between the United States, Israel and Iran.

Houthi attacks disabled the pipeline although reports from a week ago suggest it is being used again. And thanks to the Houthis, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — which means "gate of tears" in English — is also coming under pressure.

Andrew Leber, a nonresident scholar in the Middle East program of the US think tank, the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, calls it a "one-two punch of pipeline attacks and Red Sea seizures." In fact, it may send the Saudis back to the Strait of Hormuz to try to ship their oil, even though that route is still heavily restricted.

Who will help?

It is unlikely that Saudi ally, the US, is going to send help. Washington has said it will support the Saudis with intelligence and reconnaissance, but President Donald Trump appears reluctant to get involved in a direct military campaign against the Houthis.

According to a US-based think tank, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, this may partially be because the it is feeling the strain of its ongoing campaign against Iran.

"The US military is reportedly facing serious challenges, including shortages of some sophisticated interceptors," the CSIS wrote in a commentary last week.

The US Council on Foreign Relations, or CFR, has also written about dwindling stocks of Patriot and interceptor missiles, as well as cruise missiles.

So the risk of opening another front in its war with Iran, in Yemen, is not a welcome prospect for the US.

As it is, US airstrikes are unlikely to resolve the Houthi problem anyway. The CFR writes that to defuse the Houthi threat, a large, coordinated ground operation is needed, especially if forces want to push the Yemeni militia back out of the areas they recently took around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi Arabia is not too enthusiastic about this either. Despite help from the US and neighboring United Arab Emirates, a Saudi coalition that fought against the Houthis between 2015 and 2022 failed to achieve any kind of decisive victory. It also demonstrated the limits of Saudi military power.

There's clear military asymmetry. Saudi Arabia possesses modern weapons and spends enormous sums on its armed forces. But the Houthis don't need to win a conventional war. It is enough for them to use missiles and drones to threaten infrastructure and disrupt shipping.

"The Houthis are well-established in Yemen and can withstand considerable blows," Schneider told DW. "Saudi Arabia, on the other hand, needs stability above all for its 2030 economic vision. And this is currently further away than ever."

Help from the Europeans?

Since early 2024, through what is known as Operation Aspides, Europe has been protecting international shipping in the Red Sea. Italy has recently said it intends to secure passage for its own merchant ships with its navy. And a few days ago France said it would send soldiers, radar systems and air defense to the Saudis in order to protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, the terminus of the East-West pipeline.

Still, these European initiatives are unlikely to bring about any sort of strategic shift in Yemen. And experts argue Europe is unwilling to accept the political and military cost of a protracted war there.

"The fact that France has now announced it will provide concrete military assistance has been received very positively in Riyadh," Schneider explained. "But still the question remains as to whether this can fundamentally alter the military balance."

The recently formed mutual defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey, known as the Mecca alliance, also has its limits. The military leaders of all three countries have consulted with one another over recent Houthis attacks but Turkey and Pakistan are also reluctant to be drawn into a conflict that would see them confronting Iran directly.

Diplomacy the way forward

All this means that diplomatic overtures will likely become more important again.

In a previous interview with DW, Abdulghani al-Iryani of the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies noted that the Houthis do actually have an interest in relations with Saudi Arabia.

"Yemen is completely economically dependent on Saudi Arabia, both as a source of humanitarian aid and as a labor market for Yemeni migrant workers," al-Iryani said.

In recent years, Saudi Arabia has tried to curb the Houthis' influence through diplomacy and by uniting divided Yemeni government forces. However the militia's current advance seems to demonstrate the limitations of this strategy.

This story was originally published in German.

entries.title: Germany debates alleged antisemitism in the Left Party
entries.summary: The Central Council of Jews in Germany thinks the Left Party is dangerous. Other Jews, however, are showing solidarity with the party. How does that add up?
entries.content:
Germany

Do Jewish representatives see the Left Party as antisemitic?

September 30, 2026

The Central Council of Jews in Germany thinks the Left Party is dangerous. Other Jews, however, are showing solidarity with the party. How does that add up?

The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election on September 20. This means there's a good chance that the party's top candidate, Elif Eralp, could become Berlin's next mayor — making her the first member of the Left Party to hold that office.

Preliminary talks with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the environmentalist Green Party are scheduled to take place on October 1. If the talks are successful, it would represent a major step toward forming a coalition government.

Securing a clear commitment from the Left Party against antisemitism within its own ranks is seen as a prerequisite for successful cooperation. Yet doubts still persist about whether the party and its representatives can adequately protect Jewish life in the city.

During the election campaign, a performance at a Left Party event by the rapper Dahabflex made headlines and sparked outrage when he used slogans seen as antisemitic during his performance. And later, at an event held by the Left Party to celebrate its election victory, an appearance was made by Ibrahim Ibrahim — a supporter of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which is on the EU's list of terrorist organizations. The leaders of the Left Party have repeatedly distanced themselves from both incidents, both at the federal and state levels.

The Central Council of Jews in Germany is warning

However, Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, thinks these statements are mere lip service.

"In the fight against antisemitism, which is tolerated and allowed to run rampant within the party's ranks, the Left Party no longer has any credibility," reads a press statement released two days after the election. Schuster explicitly appealed to the SPD and the Greens not to form a coalition with the election winner.

High-ranking members of the federal government have also spoken out. Wolfram Weimer, government commissioner for culture and media who has no party affiliation, accused the Left Party of "openly flaunting antisemitism" and called into question the €2.9 billion ($3.3 billion) in funding for the capital's cultural sector for the coming decade — a deal that had already been agreed upon with the Berlin state government. Weimer claimed that many figures in the cultural sector are alarmed by the prospect of a government led by the Left Party.

'Antisemitism and expropriations threaten the economy'

Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, from the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), also voiced concern. A video titled "Antisemitism and Expropriations Threaten the Economy" is available on her ministry's Instagram account, in reference also to the Left Party's plans to nationalize large private housing companies.

Reiche describes the Left as a party "that openly embraces antisemitism, that instills fear in the Jews of this city, that opposes Jewish life and that cheerfully welcomes organized crime at election parties."

The Left Party is now seeking an injunction to compel the Minister of Economic Affairs to delete the video.

"Reiche is using taxpayer money to spread propaganda against the Left Party on the Economy Ministry's official channel," said Left Party Federal Co-Chair Ines Schwerdtner.

150 prominent Jews come to the defense of the Left Party

In an open letter, a group of 150 prominent Jews from various social backgrounds has voiced support for the Left Party. Among those who signed it are the author Eva Menasse and the former director of the Einstein Forum in Potsdam, Susan Neiman. They advocate for a "social and safe city" and emphasize the importance of voting for different parties.

They explain their motivation as follows: "We are writing this letter because, over the past few weeks, we have heard the same claim time and again: that the Left is dangerous for Jews, and that a coalition involving the party poses a danger to our safety. We reject this claim not because we downplay concerns about our safety, but because we actually take them seriously."

Without naming the party directly, the signatories of the letter wrote that they believe that the greatest enemy of Jewish life is the Alternative for Germany (AfD): "At a time when an in-parts openly fascistic political party is marching towards power across Germany, it is an abdication of responsibility on the part of mainstream media and elements of our own community to continue to pretend that the Left presents the largest threat to Jewish safety."

In light of this, the letter states: "The constant accusations of antisemitism against the Left are not only cynical political weaponization, but they also conflate nearly any criticism of Israel with antisemitism."

The Left Party is the only party in the German parliament that opposes arms deliveries to Israel due to the military operation in the Gaza Strip following the terrorist attack by the radical Islamist group Hamas on October 7, 2023. Based on a resolution passed at its party convention, the Left Party classifies the ensuing war as a genocide.

Elif Eralp wants to build bridges

Human rights organizations and a United Nations (UN) commission have also classified Israel's actions in Gaza against the Palestinian people as a genocide. The Israeli government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, has invoked Israel's right to self-defense.

The intensifying debate over antisemitism within the Left Party is complicating the formation of a government in Berlin. At a party congress convened on short notice, Elif Eralp, the potential future mayor of Berlin, emphasized that her party has a duty to bring people together and build bridges.

"And in doing so," Eralp said, "it must be absolutely clear that there must never be any calls for violence, and that statements that frighten Jewish people must never be made from our platforms."

With these remarks, Eralp once again criticized the antisemitic rapper's performance during the Berlin election campaign. Jewish people must be able to feel safe in Berlin, said Eralp.

"I will strengthen Berlin's diverse Jewish community and combat antisemitism. And Palestinian and Muslim people must also feel seen and safe," Eralp said.

Outside the building where the special party convention was held, about 20 Jewish people expressed their solidarity with the party. A poster in Hebrew and German lay at their feet, reading, "Mazel Tov to the Left," congratulating the party on its September 20 election victory in Berlin.

One of the demonstrators was Scott Grabell, an artist originally from New York.

"Antisemitism is real — we know that," Grabell told DW. "But three years of genocide are also real, as are illegal occupation, forced destruction and displacement in the West Bank — that, too, is real."

Grabell emphasized that they were there to support the Left Party in its efforts to advance progressive policies. "We also want to show the diversity of Jewish life in German society. Everyone talks about the different sides — we are also part of Jewish life."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Senegal's Youth Olympics makes Olympics in Africa 'logical'
entries.summary: The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.
entries.content:
September 30, 2026

The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.

At the end of October 2026, the first ever Olympic event on African soil will take place as the Youth Olympics comes to Senegal.

Around 2,700 young athletes are expected to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports, with many qualifying through the African Youth Games last year.

"We were entrusted with hosting this event and that is why from Johannesburg to Nairobi, from Dakar to Djbouti, it is all of young Africa that is watching you and watching you with pride," Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye said at the arrival of the flame.

The moment marks yet another step forward for global sport in Africa. In 2025, the first major road cycling event took place on the continent, and in September this year it was announced the first-ever World Athletics Championships would be held in Kenya in 2029. There are also on-going negotiations about Formula 1 returning. It appears that 16 years on since the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, global sport is finally returning to different parts of Africa.

"This is a victory for Africa. It opens the door for Africa to host major events," Malick Diouf, head of a marketing agency and founder of the Dakar Sport Summit, told DW.

"Africa is in the process of opening up to the world, hosting major events and everything. And all of Africa must celebrate this kind of victory."

With more major events in Africa, the question around an Olympic Games being on the continent looms.

Sports scientist Kamilla Swart has said awarding Africa a Games would make the world "take Africa more seriously." Diouf believes it's the logical next step.

"The Youth Olympic Games, it's a major test for Africa. And I think this is where we need to succeed in organizing these Games and also in sending a message," Diouf said.

"We, Africa, are ready to host the Summer Olympics, and I think that would be the logical next step after the Dakar Olympics. We have Olympic champions; we have record holders; we have Olympians, so we deserve to host the Olympic Games."

Senegal an attractive option for many reasons

The move to re-use and refurbish existing facilities rather than build whole new ones is likely why Senegal's bid was so tempting for the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

The fear of the white elephant facility appears to have been considered here. The Iba Mar Diop Stadium, the track and field stadium, is expected to be used for athlete training ahead of the 2028 Olympics.

"It’s by using these facilities, by participating in and hosting international events, and by consistently maintaining them to the required standards, that we’ll be able to keep these stadiums up to the standards they currently meet," Diouf said.

There's also the social and economical impacts of the Youth Olympics. Diouf believes the impact is beyond just infrastructure, but into roads, the development of the hospitality, security and broadcasting sectors and the young athletes themselves.

"There's life after the Games. Now we need to figure out how to use the resources we have, we need to develop and capitalize on what we have showcased during the Games," said Diouf.

Future of Youth Olympics in doubt

The significance of these Games stretch beyond even the history they are making in Africa. In May of this year, IOC President Kirsty Coventry put the brakes on the future of the Youth Olympics, leaving real doubts as to whether there will be any more after the 2028 winter edition.

"We need to pause and have a real reflection on why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games and we realized that across the Movement it's very disjointed. There's not a true North Star of why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games," Coventry told reporters.

"So the EB (IOC Executive Board) decided to pause the 2030 process right now so there will not be an election in June, and rather we need to take a step back and develop a youth strategy."

A lot has changed since the Youth Olympic Games were launched in 2010. Initially it was seen as a way to engage a younger audience (athletes were limited by age to between 15 and 18) by trialing new sports as well as testing host country's on a smaller stage. However, with the age of athletes decreasing and the challenges of engaging a younger audience in the modern sports entertainment landscape even more challenging, it appears clear the IOC are reconsidering their options when it comes to investment.

"My only wish is that Dakar be memorable and that people reconsider their decision not to host the Games in 2030," Diouf said.

"I don’t want these to be the last Youth Olympic Games, but if these are to be the last Youth Olympic Games, we need to go out with a bang. Dakar needs to show the world what Senegal is all about, what Africa is all about."

From October 31 to November 13 this year, Senegal will have the chance to do just that.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: African leaders herald $16B Dangote oil refinery in Kenya
entries.summary: An oil refinery on Kenya's coast is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote, will lead the project.
entries.content:
September 30, 2026

An oil refinery on Kenya's coast is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote, will lead the project.

African leaders on Wednesday broke ground on a new $16 billion (€14 billion) oil refinery off Kenya's coast.

The project is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. The refinery will be constructed at the coastal town of Lamu.

Kenya's President William Ruto, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed were among the leaders who attended an event to celebrate the project, the largest of its kind in East and Central Africa. 

The refinery "will strengthen regional energy security, reduce reliance on imports and bolster our foreign exchange," Ruto said on social media.

"But this is more than a refinery. It is an integrated industrial complex featuring a 1,000MW power plant, plastic factory and the manufacturing of fertilizers and chemicals."

Africa's richest man, Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote, will oversee the project.

Dangote: Project will reduce refined fuel imports, foster self-sufficiency

Dangote said the refinery will make East Africa more "self-sufficient" by reducing imports of refined fuel.

"For too long, our continent has actually been rich in resources but poor in value creation and addition. We have exported crude oil and imported refined products," Dangote said in his speech.

"Such practice only leads to us exporting our jobs and opportunities that should remain on the continent and lead us into importing poverty into our nations. Africa cannot build lasting prospertiy by exporting what it has and importing what it needs," he continued.

Lamu project faces environmental concerns, legal challenge

The project, however, has faced resistance from environmental campaigners who fear it could harm Lamu Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site which also hosts a fragile and unique marine ecosystem.

The Lamu marine environment is also home to animals such as dugongs, whales and various sea turtle species.

Lamu residents have brought a land rights legal case against the refinery, saying the site where it will be built is their ancestral heritage.

Kenya's High Court on Monday ruled that legal proceedings will continue, but the groundbreaking ceremony can take place.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Flydubai pilot investigated over possible attempt to crash Tel Aviv-bound flight
entries.summary: A Flydubai service from the UAE to Israel made an emergency landing after one pilot stabbed another. Officials are investigating whether this was a deliberate attempt to crash the plane.
entries.content:
Israel

Flydubai pilot stabbed en route to Israel

Published September 30, 2026last updated September 30, 2026

A Flydubai service from the UAE to Israel made an emergency landing after one pilot stabbed another. Officials are investigating whether this was a deliberate attempt to crash the plane.

Authorities are investigating whether a Flydubai pilot tried to crash an Israel-bound flight after it plummeted several thousand feet on Wednesday.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that one pilot had stabbed another pilot mid-flight, forcing the plane to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. Flydubai confirmed that all passengers were safe.

Israel's defense minister, Israel Katz, said that "an attempted jihadist terror attack" had been thwarted after several passengers intervened.

A spokesperson for the prime minister's office said that Netanyahu has ordered authorities to "ramp up" security on both Israeli and non-Israeli carriers following the Flydubai flight incident.

On Wednesday evening, passengers from the diverted Flydubai flight arrived in Israel on a replacement plane, where numerous relatives were waiting for them.

What happened on the Flydubai flight?

Flydubai said flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv experienced an "incident" while en route and landed safely in northwestern Saudi Arabia. The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 8.

"The aircraft has landed safely in Tabuk Airport and all passengers are safe and accounted for," a Flydubai spokesperson said.

Later, a Flydubai spokesperson said that the reasons for an altercation that "occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073" remained unknown and were under formal investigation.

"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation. We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts," a spokesperson said in a statement published by the AFP news agency.

Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported that authorities were investigating whether one of the pilots had deliberately tried to crash the aircraft, with the other pilot intervening to stop him.

Israeli media said one of the pilots suffered a stab wound. Initial reports had described the incident only as a fight between the two pilots, but images later published by Israeli outlets appeared to show a passenger with blood on his shirt.

Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 initially showed a second Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, FZ1081, diverting back toward Dubai. It later showed the aircraft continuing toward Tel Aviv. There was no immediate explanation for the change.

How far did the plane fall?

The Israeli news portal Ynet reported that the aircraft entered a steep descent and that passengers helped one pilot prevent the other from crashing the plane.

Flight tracking data shows the aircraft suddenly losing around half its altitude as it neared Saudi Arabia's border with Jordan.

The plane dropped from nearly 34,000 feet (10,360 meters) at 05:21 GMT/UTC to below 17,000 feet (5,180 meters) at 05:22 GMT/UTC, according to Flightradar data.

Israel's Kan public broadcaster and Channel 12 reported that the Israeli military scrambled fighter jets amid initial fears of a possible hijacking. That possibility was later dismissed, according to the reports.

Israeli minister says 'attempted jihadist terror attack' thwarted

Israeli leaders announced that a "jihadist" pilot had attempted to crash a Flydubai plane carrying mostly Israeli passengers.

In a video message, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that "during the flight... one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone on board."

He added that passengers and crew subdued the attacker, and the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, where the pilot was arrested.

"I salute these heroes who showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage. They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster," Netanyahu said.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz described the incident as "an attempted jihadist terror attack" that was "thwarted only thanks to the heroism of several Israeli passengers."

Earlier, Netanyahu's office said he had held consultations over the incident and was monitoring developments.

"The incident is under control, and all measures are currently being deployed in order to return the Israeli passengers safely to Israel," his office said.

An unnamed senior Israeli government official told Channel 12 that a major disaster had been averted.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

Edited by: Zac Crellin, Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Iran's nuclear program remains shrouded in mystery as the regime debates ditching non-proliferation
entries.summary: Iran's nuclear program is entering a critical phase as Tehran debates dropping out of a nuclear non-proliferation treaty. Satellite images also show activity at known nuclear sites.
entries.content:
Asia

What is Iran's nuclear endgame?

September 30, 2026

Iran's nuclear program is entering a critical phase as Tehran debates dropping out of a nuclear non-proliferation treaty. Satellite images also show activity at known nuclear sites.

Iran's nuclear program has entered one of the most critical periods in its history.

Questions over Tehran's stockpile of uranium enriched to 60% and the International Atomic Energy Agency's (IAEA) declining oversight of Iranian nuclear facilities have only deepened the uncertainty. Yet signs of diplomacy remain.

In an interview last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told US broadcaster Fox News that Tehran is prepared to dilute its enriched uranium stockpile and submit its nuclear program for international inspection, provided a comprehensive agreement is reached within the framework of international law and the landmark Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT). 

Conflicting statements from Iran

However, in contrast to Pezeshkian's diplomatic rhetoric, statements from military and political figures in Tehran point in a different direction.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said that US and Israeli actions had created grounds for Iran to withdraw from the NPT, while stressing that no decision had yet been made, according to Press TV, the Iranian government's main English-language satellite TV channel.

On September 19, British newspaper The Daily Telegraph, citing satellite imagery, reported that Iran was actively constructing new facilities and rebuilding damaged ones.

These sites include "Taleghan 2" at the Parchin complex southeast of Tehran and a complex burrowed under what is known as Pickaxe Mountain near Iran's nuclear facility in Natanz.

Both sites were previously targeted in airstrikes during the US-Israel war with Iran, which the Pentagon dubbed Operation Epic Fury and Israel called Operation Roaring Lion.

Their reported reconstruction has fueled speculation that equipment and enriched uranium may have been moved deeper underground.

Washington has maintained a firm stance. Speaking at the UN General Assembly on September 22, US President Donald Trump said: "I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon."

Can diplomacy still work?

Access to military sites and the scope of IAEA inspections have long been among the most contentious issues related to Iran's nuclear program.

The 2015 nuclear agreement known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) imposed significant restrictions on Iran, in exchange for sanctions relief, to prevent it from developing nuclear weapons.

However, provisions for the inspection of military sites drew persistent criticism from opponents in Washington, criticism that contributed to the US withdrawal from the JCPOA under Donald Trump in 2018.

John Bolton, former US national security adviser and former US ambassador to the UN, told DW that diplomatic efforts and past agreements on Iran's nuclear program are merely a "cover for an unalterable strategy pursued by Tehran."

Arguing that Iran's weapons program was "never" truly halted, Bolton pointed to what he described as the limitations of international institutions, adding that "the IAEA never had access to Iran's military bases, where critical components related to weaponization take place."

When asked about the legal implications of a potential Iranian withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation Treaty, Bolton argued that Iran has been in violation of the NPT for more than three decades, meaning a formal withdrawal would make little practical difference.

"The only long-term path to achieving peace and security in the Middle East," Bolton emphasized, "is the overthrow of the regime in Tehran."

War steels Tehran's nuclear resolve

Amid the US-Israel war with Iran and the subsequent changes in Tehran's command structure after the death of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, fresh developments have emerged.

The IAEA Board of Governors referred Iran to the UN Security Council on September 9 over alleged breaches of its non-proliferation obligations.

Meanwhile, the 60-day period for technical talks with the United States under the so-called Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, which extended a ceasefire between the two sides, expired in mid-August.

Damon Golriz, a political analyst and lecturer at The Hague University of Applied Sciences, argues that, contrary to Donald Trump's view of his legacy in dismantling Iran's nuclear capabilities, a nuclear-armed Iran would ultimately prove to be "the greatest foreign policy legacy of Donald Trump's presidency."

Reflecting on the military developments of 2026 and the killing of Khamenei in an Israeli air strike, Golriz said: "In February 2026 Tehran faced an existential war."

"The campaign entombed its nuclear facilities and decapitated its key weapons scientists, along with at least five tiers of Iran's top military and security establishment," Golriz added.

"Israel's killing of the supreme leader settled a fundamental security question: Has Ayatollah Khamenei as the main constraint on Iran's nuclear bomb became obsolete?"

Golriz suggests that it was specifically the audacity shown in the targeting of Iran's leadership that upended the country's national security thinking, thereby "strengthening calls to reassess its nuclear doctrine."

Testing Tehran's religious rhetoric on nukes

The official religious decree, or fatwa, banning the production and stockpiling of nuclear weapons has long been a cornerstone of Tehran's diplomatic rhetoric in claiming its nuclear program is peaceful.

First cited by Iranian officials in the mid-2000s, the fatwa was reaffirmed by Khamenei in 2019, when he said producing and stockpiling nuclear weapons was forbidden.

However, amid political developments in Tehran and Mojtaba Khamenei's silence on reaffirming this fatwa since becoming the new supreme leader, questions have been raised whether this religious red line remains intact or has given way to new security considerations.

Tim Bosch, CEO of the Birdwatcher Group and a former senior intelligence officer with the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD), pointed to the significance of this silence alongside rhetoric from military figures in Tehran.

Bosch told DW that there is no definitive proof of a formal change in Tehran's nuclear doctrine.

"However, those opposed to acquiring nuclear weapons in Tehran are now far weaker, and given Mojtaba Khamenei's silence in reiterating his father's fatwa, this observation carries significant weight," he said.

In December 2024, the IAEA assessed that Iran was the only country without a nuclear bomb to posses uranium enriched to 60%, while warning Tehran was "dramatically accelerating" enrichment. A purity of 90% is needed to produce nuclear weapons.

However, with the IAEA barred from inspections, it is anyone's guess as to how far along Iran currently is.

"If the world's nuclear watchdog cannot observe enriched uranium, no intelligence agency can honestly claim to know whether Iran has made the final decision to build a bomb," Bosch said.

"Those who claim with absolute certainty that 'they have made their decision' are either bluffing or mostly advancing their own political agendas: hardliners in Iran on one side, and hardliners in Israel and the United States on the other," he added.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Lawyer of Junaid Hafeez, a Pakistai scholar imprisoned for 13 years, is hopeful for his release
entries.summary: A former Fullbright scholar, Junaid Hafeez was sentenced to death under Pakistan's controversial blasphemy laws. His family and lawyer told DW there is now hope a court will overturn the conviction.
entries.content:
September 30, 2026

A former Fullbright scholar, Junaid Hafeez was sentenced to death under Pakistan's controversial blasphemy laws. His family and lawyer told DW there is now hope a court will overturn the conviction.

Junaid Hafeez, a former university lecturer and Fullbright scholar was thrown in prison 13 years ago under Pakistan's strict blasphemy laws for comments he allegedly made on Facebook.  After a trial that spanned years, a court in 2019 sentenced him to death.

Last week, a high court in Lahore began hearing Hafeez's appeal, raising hopes his conviction could be overturned.

"I want to see my son free and back home. We are fighting a very difficult battle," Junaid Hafeez's father, Hafeez-un-Naseer, told DW.

Naseer said he met with his son in prison last Thursday through a glass window, speaking to him by phone.

"This case has taken everything from us," he said.

Saif-ul-Malook, a lawyer representing Hafeez, said the academic has read thousands of books during his years in prison.

"He is an intellectual. His health is fine, but he is frustrated inside the jail," Malook told DW. "I am hopeful that under this bench, he will be released."

Who is Junaid Hafeez?

Before his arrest, Hafeez was a Fulbright scholar and had studied in the United States. He later returned to Pakistan and began working as a lecturer in English literature at Bahauddin Zakariya University in the city of Multan.

Human rights groups say that shortly after he began working there as a graduate student in 2011, he found himself targeted by an Islamist student group who took issue with what they considered Hafeez's "liberal" teaching.

Hafeez was arrested on March 13, 2013, accused of using a fake Facebook profile to insult the Prophet Muhammad in a closed group called "So-Called Liberals of Pakistan."

His father has said he was set up by the Islamists on campus, who wanted to get one of their own into an open position at the university.

What are the details of the blasphemy case?

His trial began in 2014. Because of security concerns, legal proceedings were later moved to Multan Central Jail, and were repeatedly delayed until he was sentenced to death by a trial court in Multan. Hafeez challenged the verdict in 2020, and his appeal has yet to be decided.

The Lahore High Court heard Hafeez's appeal on September 22 before a two-member bench. The judges issued notices to the prosecution and the complainant and asked for arguments on the electronic evidence being relied upon in the case. This includes Facebook material attributed to Hafeez.

"Lahore High Court judges have generally been reluctant to hear blasphemy appeals. This time, Justice Sadiq Mahmud Khurram is on the bench. Let's see how he approaches the case. In my experience, there is prejudice against the accused at every stage," Malook said.

Pakistan's blasphemy laws in focus

Hafiz Ehtisham Ahmed, an Islamabad-based Islamic activist, told DW he thinks the court should uphold the blasphemy conviction, arguing abolishing the laws could "encourage disrespect for religion."

"There is international pressure on Pakistan to change these laws. If Hafeez is acquitted, it would raise serious questions about the justice system," Ahmed said.

Strict blasphemy laws in Muslim-majority Pakistan have been widely condemned internationally for their arbitrary applicaiton and the potential for abuse of power. 

Pakistani policy analyst Raza Rumi said that judges are under intense pressure when handling blasphemy cases.

"Acquittals or even procedural decisions can trigger threats and public backlash, contributing to delays and caution in handling such cases," Rumi told DW.

Security has been a major issue throughout the proceedings.

"Human rights groups have documented threats against judges, lawyers, and prosecutors in blasphemy cases. Concerns over their safety can affect both the pace of proceedings and judicial independence," Rumi added.

At least seven judges were transferred during the trial. Hafeez's first lawyer, Rashid Rehman, was shot dead in his Multan office in May 2014. He had reportedly received threats in connection with the case.

What are the chances for Hafeez's appeal?

Hafeez can still be released if the Lahore High Court overturns his conviction. But that will depend on the judges' assessment of the evidence and the arguments made during the appeal. A death sentence imposed by a trial court does not become final without scrutiny by the high court.

For Hafeez, the question now is how quickly the Lahore High Court can hear and decide his appeal after years of delays. The next hearing is due on October 10, but it is unclear how long it will take the court to decide.

"We wish that one night we could go to sleep and wake up to find our son free and back home," said father Naseer.

"I still remember the pain we have endured over all these years since my son was falsely accused. Thirteen years have taken so much from our family, but we have never stopped hoping that one day Junaid will walk free," Naseer added.

Human Rights Watch (HRW) has called for the blasphemy conviction to be overturned. In a February press statement, HRW called for Hafeez's release, adding he has been kept in solitary confinement since June 2014.

"If his appeal is rejected, Junaid's mother will not survive it. His father can barely walk. The whole family has been destroyed. If released, I believe Junaid will become an internationally recognized intellectual, lecturing at leading universities," said lawyer Malook.

"We hope that Hafeez's remaining life will not be wasted in the prison on the death row and [that his] case will be finally concluded and he will be acquitted," Malookadded.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Manchester City Premier League charges: What do they mean?
entries.summary: Since being bought by the UAE in 2008, Manchester City have become one of the world's most successful football clubs. A raft of serious financial charges threatens to undermine this and bring chaos to the Premier League.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

Manchester City Premier League charges: What do they mean?

September 30, 2026

Since being bought by the UAE in 2008, Manchester City have become one of the world's most successful football clubs. A raft of serious financial charges threatens to undermine this and bring chaos to the Premier League.

Manchester City have won the Premier League eight times over the last 14 years. But whether those titles will remain is one of a plethora of issues at stake after England's top division charged one of its most high profile clubs with more than 100 breaches of its financial regulations.

On Tuesday, the Premier League announced that an independent commission had found City had drawn up "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs". These contracts, dubious sponsorships and a number of other methods were, according to the commission's report, used to inflate the club's revenue to the tune of about £900 million (€1.05 billion) over the period between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

The case has been ongoing for eight years after initial revelations from Germany's Der Spiegel and Rui Pinto of the 'Football Leaks' website. City continue to deny any wrongdoing.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case," read a City statement. "Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."

What was the Premier League verdict on the Manchester City charges?

The 750-page report was damning, accusing City of inflating contracts and sponsorship deals, running secondary contracts off book, making "concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation" and signing off inflated image rights deals to artificially boost their earnings. All this enabled them to pass both Premier League and UEFA financial spending limits, states the report.

The Premier League's chief ­executive, Richard Masters, described the case "as the most significant in Premier League history," adding that the club "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade."

Though the Premier League, the most commercially successful football league in the world, has drawn some praise for its actions, others point to the fact that it took Pinto leaking emails and media reports to force any action. The report shows that City, who had won the league once in 71 years before being taken over by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2008, were consistently posting revenues way higher than any of their more established and successful rivals.

Who are the key figures at Manchester City?

In this context, its the owners. The Abu Dhabi United Group, essentially an investment vehicle for the UAE royal family, bought the club in 2008. The takeover was fronted by Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, know simply as Sheikh Mansour. He is a member of the ruling Al Nahyan family and the UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who also holds a number of government positions in the UAE, was brought in as chairman.

Nation state ownership of this type is controversial in European football and City's owners have long been criticized for the country's human rights record and using the club for sportswashing. Similar criticisms have been made of European champions Paris Saint-Germain (Qatar) and City's Premier League rivals Newcastle United (Saudi Arabia).

City's CEO, Ferran Soriano, joined in 2012 as City expanded their ownership into foreign leagues, buying up clubs in the US, Japan and Australia. He replaced former head coach Roberto Mancini with fellow Spaniard Manuel Pellegrini before former Bayern Munich and Barcelona coach Pep Guardiola took over in 2016, ushering in the club's most successful period.

How did Manchester City's system work?

The club immediately started splashing out on big money transfers on the arrival of UAE investment. At that point, neither UEFA nor the Premier League had the tight financial rules they now have. UEFA's Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules were brought in for the 2011-12 season while the Premier League followed with its Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) in 2013-14.

City's free spending and relative lack of commercial income meant they were likely to fall foul of such rules. The club were handed a conditional €60 million UEFA fine for losses in the 2011-12 and 2012-13 seasons. They would later be banned from the Champions League on similar grounds in 2020 before being reinstated on appeal.

In an attempt to try and comply with such financial rules, City set up a system they called 'Project Longbow' in 2012. The commission said much of this was genuine but one arm of it was an agreement with a a third party called Fordham which was, according to the ruling, "little more than a front." Essentially, it reads, the club's UAE owners "would be used (and were used) to enable Fordham to acquire from the club (at a sizeable, artificially-inflated price) the club's entitlement to benefit financially from its players' image rights."

In other words, City's owners were pumping money in to their own club through vastly inflated sponsorship and image rights deals so their income looked higher and they could spend more, particularly on player transfers and wages. The report also claims that City paid three individuals, whose names are redacted, through a third party to keep them off the books.

What happens next?

That's the question on everyone's lips. As yet, no sanctions have been laid against City and the appeal will likely drag proceedings out even longer. Meanwhile the club, who are top of the Premier League, face Liverpool on October 11, after the international break.

While there is no precedent for such a tranche of charges, clubs have fallen foul of the Premier League's PSR regulations before. Everton were handed a 10-point penalty for a £19.5-million(€22.8 million) breach over a period ending with the 2021-22 season. This was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach, plus an additional point for every £5 million the club overspent. Given that City's overspending is close to a billion pounds, applying that would certainly relegate them, though the division below, the Championship, is not operated by the Premier League.

For now, it looks like City and the league will play on under a cloud. But if the verdict remains after appeal, clubs and individuals whose careers and honors stand to be impacted, will likely come forward and litigate. City themselves could be relegated, docked points over successive seasons, face transfer bans or any combination of those things. The titles won in the relevant period could also be stripped.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold
